title: Per-Trial Swap Grids
takeaway: This is the trial-by-trial record behind the flexible-generalization headline count: sixteen small grids, one per function template, showing what the model actually said after every individual lens-coordinate swap. It exposes a sharp gradient the summary number hides - country swaps redirect the answer almost perfectly at 42 of 48 off-diagonal cells, while number relations succeed on none of 48 at standard strength. The grey ranks in the failing cells show the target answer usually sits somewhere below the top rather than absent, which is the paper's evidence that weak swaps push in the right direction without going far enough.
walkthrough:
This item unpacks the summary counts of the [[flexible-generalization]] experiment into the individual trials that produced them; the article renders it as a live widget rather than a static image. It holds sixteen small grids, one per function template of the [[function-template-protocol]] - four templates in each of four argument categories: countries, months, animals, and number words.

Each grid is $4 \times 4$, because its category supplies four arguments. A row fixes the argument actually written in the prompt. A column fixes the argument whose [[j-lens-vector]] is swapped in.

The intervention is the [[lens-coordinate-swap]]: the activation's coordinates along the row vector and the column vector are read, exchanged, and written back, held at every token position across a band of middle layers ([[activation-clamping]]). Each column carries a sub-heading giving the answer that this template implies for the swapped-in argument. Under the template "the capital of ___ is", the column for China is headed with Beijing.

The four cells on the diagonal are those where row and column name the same argument. Nothing is exchanged there, so the diagonal is the unmodified baseline. The twelve off-diagonal cells are the real trials. Four grids at twelve trials each gives 48 per category, and sixteen grids give 192 in all.

A cell prints the model's top-1 output token after the swap. The trial counts as a success when that token is the column's sub-heading. Where it is not, a small grey number gives the rank of the target-appropriate answer in the output distribution; the number is omitted at rank 1 because the printed token already shows it.

Read across categories, the grids separate cleanly. Country swaps land on 42 of 48 off-diagonal cells. Months succeed partially, animals rarely, and number relations on 0 of 48. The four categories together make up the 76 of 192 successes reported in the main text, so months and animals account for 34 of their shared 96 trials; the paper gives the ordering rather than the two separate counts.

The grey ranks carry a second point. Among the failures, the top-1 token is typically still the correct answer for the argument written in the prompt, and the target's answer appears further down. All grids are at standard swap strength. Doubling it to $\alpha = 2$ ([[swap-strength-alpha]]) often brings the target answer up, and the paper reads the ranks and that recovery together as a swap that moves the activation the right way but not far enough. The category gradient itself tracks [[workspace-loading]], which is highest for countries and lowest for number words. The model is Claude Sonnet 4.5 ([[claude-model-family]]).

terms.definition: One $4 \times 4$ block of cells covering every ordered pair of arguments for a single function template. Sixteen grids appear, four for each argument category.
A prompt frame applying one fixed operation to a slotted argument, such as "the capital of ___ is" or "most people in ___ speak". Each grid belongs to exactly one template.
The source argument: the word actually written into the template on that trial, and the concept whose lens coordinate the swap removes.
The target argument: the concept whose J-lens vector is written into the activation in the source's place. The model is never shown this word.
Printed under each column: the answer the template implies for the swapped-in argument. It is the token a cell must show for the trial to count as a success.
A cell where row and column name the same argument, so the swap exchanges a coordinate with itself and changes nothing. The four diagonal cells of a grid are its unmodified baseline.
A cell where source and target differ - an actual swap trial. Twelve per grid, 48 per category, 192 overall, and the only cells the success counts are computed over.
The model's single most likely next token after the swap has been applied and the forward pass completed. This is what the grid reports for each trial.
The rank of the target-appropriate answer in the model's output distribution, shown only when that rank is not 1. Its presence marks a failed trial and its size says how badly the swap missed.
Position of a token in the model's output distribution ordered by probability. Rank 1 is the top-1 token; rank 7 means six tokens were more likely.

The intervention behind every off-diagonal cell: the residual stream's coordinates along the source and target J-lens vectors are read via a pseudoinverse, exchanged, and written back, leaving the rest of the activation untouched.
The direction in activation space that the Jacobian lens associates with one vocabulary token. Rows and columns are indexed by arguments, but the swap operates on these vectors.
Enforcing the swapped coordinates at every token position and every layer in the chosen band for the whole forward pass, rather than editing once and letting the value drift.
The argument category with the highest workspace loading and the best results here: 42 of its 48 off-diagonal cells show the target-appropriate answer at rank 1.
The second argument category. Its grids show partial success - some cells flip to the target answer, others do not.
The third argument category, where swaps rarely redirect the answer; most off-diagonal cells still print the answer for the argument in the prompt.
The number-word category, whose functions are arithmetic or ordering relations over small integers. No off-diagonal cell succeeds at standard swap strength.
The output the template implies for the swapped-in argument - Beijing rather than Paris under "the capital of ___ is". Success is defined as this token reaching rank 1.
A multiplier on the swap's magnitude. The grids are all at the default strength; at $\alpha = 2$ the source vector is subtracted and the target added at double magnitude.
The cosine similarity between the residual stream and a concept's lens vector on an unmodified forward pass. It is the quantity the paper uses to explain why the categories order as they do here.
The model whose outputs fill the cells; the paper's default subject model, with key results corroborated on Haiku 4.5 and Opus 4.5 elsewhere.

numbers.meaning: Grids in the item, one per function template: four argument categories with four functions each.
The shape of every grid. Each category supplies four arguments, and each argument can appear as a row (in the prompt) or a column (swapped in), giving sixteen cells.
Diagonal cells per grid, where source equals target. These are baselines, not trials, and are excluded from every success count.
Off-diagonal cells per grid: 16 total cells minus the 4 on the diagonal. Equivalently, each of 4 arguments can be swapped for any of the other 3.
Swap trials per argument category: 4 templates times 12 off-diagonal cells. This is the denominator in both 42/48 and 0/48.
Off-diagonal cells across the whole item: 16 grids times 12, or 4 categories times 48. The denominator for the main text's aggregate count.
Country swaps whose target-appropriate answer reaches rank 1 - about 88%. Countries have the highest workspace loading, which the paper offers as the reason.

Number-relation swaps that succeed at standard strength: none. Number words have the lowest workspace loading; the paper leaves open whether small-integer computation runs outside the workspace or merely fails to align with the number tokens' lens vectors.

The main text's aggregate over all sixteen grids at standard strength. Subtracting the 42 country successes and the 0 number successes leaves 34 across the 96 month and animal trials, which the paper does not split further.
Successes reported in the main text when the swap is run at double strength. The grids themselves are at standard strength, so this number is context rather than a quantity plotted here.
The success threshold. A cell at rank 1 prints the column sub-heading and carries no grey number; any other rank is printed in grey beside the token the model actually produced.
The double-strength condition that recovers many of the failing cells, which the paper reads as evidence that a failed swap moved the activation in the right direction but not far enough.
